Dirt Rocc on Meeting Orlando Anderson, Joining Southside Crips (Part 1)
recentItems.description:
Become a VladStocks Member now: https://www.youtube.com/vladtv/join
--------
Devonte “Dirt Rock” Lee sits down with VladTV to trace his early years around Compton, his family ties to the area, and how sports initially kept him away from street politics. He recalls meeting Orlando “Baby Lane” Anderson around 1992 or 1993, getting to know Anderson’s Southside Compton Crip family, and later being pressed by the neighborhood to decide whether he and Big Dre were going to officially join. Dirt Rock describes the one-on-one “put on” fights, hanging around lowriders, and how existing conflicts with Bloods, certain Compton Crips, and North Side Long Beach shaped his path. He also clarifies the difference between Southside Crips and L.A.’s Rollin’ 60s, mentions Big U, and talks about ties with Nutty Block Compton Crips and B.G. Knocc Out. The conversation adds context to Compton history, Orlando Anderson, and the larger 2Pac murder case narrative.

recentItems.title: Max B on Co-Defendant Gina Conway Attacked in Prison for Snitching on Him (Part 11)

Part 1: https://youtu.be/FoBBj-6j544
--------
In this VladTV interview, Harlem rapper Max B opens up about serving nearly 18 years, receiving a 20-year sentence in 2016, and staying focused on music while awaiting release. He discusses the 2021 reconciliation between French Montana and Jim Jones, calling it “love,” and reflects on how the hip-hop landscape evolved while he was incarcerated. Max B also addresses his relationship with co-defendant Gina Conway, who previously testified against him, revealing they exchanged letters in prison and that he tried to support her mental health. He says Conway was repeatedly attacked behind bars after being labeled a snitch, forcing others to step in. The conversation also covers prison violence, gang politics, avoiding conflict, and how Max B managed to keep his name and career alive from inside.

recentItems.title: TK Kirkland: Lil Durk Beat The Case Because Drew Finley & Brian Steel Are Bad A** Lawyers (Part 4)

Part 1: https://youtu.be/rRLJVBMJt3I
-------

TK Kirkland joins Vlad to break down Lil Durk’s not guilty verdict and why he believes the win came down to an elite defense team led by Drew Findling (Drew Finley) and Brian Steel. The conversation examines how prosecutors faced reasonable doubt despite multiple cooperating witnesses, while co-defendants Deedee and Brown Eyes were found guilty of murder. Vlad details the lack of a “smoking gun,” the role of testimony tied to life-sentence pressure, and how the case compares to famous criminal vs. civil outcomes like O.J. Simpson.  

The discussion also looks ahead to Durk’s pending RICO case, possible testimony from Otis “Boogie,” the fallout from King Von’s death, and whether the same prosecutors can regroup after losing a major Los Angeles federal case. TK adds street-level perspective on snitching, plea deals, ego, and why successful entertainers should leave street life behind.

--------
Trap Lore Ross joins Vlad to break down Lil Durk’s ongoing legal battle after his not-guilty verdict in the first trial, explaining why the upcoming RICO case may be far broader than many fans realize. Ross disputes online claims about double jeopardy and the Stephan Mack murder allegations, pointing to the indictment’s pages 2–11 and the Supreme Court’s Currier case as key context. The conversation covers alleged OTF connections, violent crime in aid of racketeering, the Lil Pab case, Alexander Witherspoon shooting, Quando Rondo incident in Blackshear, Georgia, and references to King Von, D Thang, Lil Tim, NBA YoungBoy, Boonie Mo, Black Disciples, and the Atlanta Varsity shooting. Vlad also raises potential witnesses including OTF Jam and Vonnie as Durk prepares for a second federal trial. A detailed legal and hip-hop analysis of one of rap’s most closely watched cases.

--------

Criminal defense attorney Bradford Cohen sits down with Vlad to break down the ethics and realities of representing clients in high-profile murder cases. Cohen discusses defending Nima Momeni in the Bob Lee case, the Cash App founder’s fatal stabbing in San Francisco, and explains why he believed the trial raised serious questions around self-defense, evidence, the missing “white car,” and potential appeal issues.

The conversation also turns to the D4vd case, where Cohen explains how he evaluates disturbing allegations, why every defendant deserves a defense, and why not every case deserves a “Brad Cohen defense.” Vlad and Cohen also analyze the Keefe D Las Vegas murder trial involving Tupac Shakur, Judge Mathis’ legal take, VladTV interview evidence, and why a 90-minute guilty verdict stood out. Cohen closes by discussing legal ethics, celebrity clients, fair representation, and what separates principled attorneys from lawyers who exploit clients.

Nicholas Irving joins Shawn Prez for a candid breakdown of why America often misunderstands the endurance of militant enemies in Afghanistan and the broader Middle East. Irving argues that for fighters who see conflict through a religious lens, military strikes, economic pressure, and even a closed strait may not create the breaking point U.S. leaders expect. The conversation explores faith, hardship, poverty, cultural resilience, and why a group conditioned by generations of extreme conditions may view surrender very differently than Americans do.

Prez and Irving also discuss U.S. comfort, short attention spans, the news cycle, President Biden’s Afghanistan withdrawal, and whether Donald Trump or future presidents will avoid owning the difficult end of America’s longest wars. A sharp, unfiltered look at modern warfare, ideology, foreign policy, and the limits of American power.

Interview by: Shawn Prez

Part 1: https://youtu.be/-pWadYhoSkc
--------
In this VladTV interview, Norteño Shot Caller Mario Sanchez gives a stark look inside California prison life, describing how violence, politics, and survival played out on active Level 4 yards and in the Corcoran SHU. Speaking with DJ Vlad, Sanchez discusses why stabbings were more common than fistfights in certain Mexican prison circles, the pressure inmates faced when ordered to act, and his own history with prison assaults. He also explains the prison culture around improvised weapons without glamorizing it, including how contraband was moved onto the yard and the slang terms “keyster,” “hoop,” and “safe.” Sanchez reflects on the discomfort, danger, and normalization of these practices behind bars, tying the conversation to his broader experiences and writings about incarceration, discipline, and the “art of war” mentality inside the system. A raw, cautionary conversation about prison reality and consequences.
